entities.summary:
Saint Judicael (c. 602 – December 20, 658), King of Domnonée in Brittany, stands as a pivotal figure in 7th-century Armorican history, embodying the complex interplay between secular authority and burgeoning Christian monasticism during the Early Middle Ages. Reigned from approximately 615 to 640, Judicael navigated the precarious geopolitical landscape of post-Roman Gaul, asserting a degree of Breton autonomy while acknowledging the suzerainty of the powerful Merovingian Frankish kingdom. His life trajectory, marked by a dramatic abdication to embrace monastic life, established him as a revered Roman Catholic saint, whose cult profoundly shaped the spiritual and cultural identity of Brittany for centuries.

His reign was primarily defined by diplomatic maneuvering, notably his significant meeting with Dagobert I, the Frankish King, around 635. This encounter, likely at Clichy or Paris, resulted in a formal submission of Domnonée to the Frankish crown, a strategic move that secured peace and prevented outright Frankish conquest, albeit at the cost of full independence. Judicael's decision to present himself before Dagobert, after an initial period of resistance and border raids, demonstrated a pragmatic leadership style aimed at preserving his kingdom's long-term stability. Following this period of political consolidation, Judicael renounced his throne around 640, choosing to enter the monastery of Saint Méen, a decision reflecting the deep spiritual currents influencing noble elites of the era.
